opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a really good question, and it's something I think about a lot. I'm a big fan of tools and retrieval because they're cheap and flexible. You don't have to retrain anything, you can swap out the knowledge source, and you get some traceability, since you can see which document the model pulled from. For things like fresh facts, today's news, or a company's internal docs, I think that's the right default.

But there are some real limits. The first is the context window itself. Even with very long contexts, there's a difference between fitting information in and the model actually using it well. Models still tend to attend unevenly; they might pick up what's at the beginning or end and miss something in the middle. And long contexts cost compute and latency on every single query, whereas knowledge in the weights is essentially free at inference time.

The second limit is that retrieval gives the model facts, not skills. If you want a model to get better at a new programming language, a new domain's style of reasoning, or a specific output format it keeps getting wrong, stuffing examples into the prompt only gets you so far. That's where fine-tuning, or even continued pre-training, still makes sense, because you're changing how the model processes information, not just what it can look up.

Third, retrieval is only as good as the retrieval step. If the search pulls the wrong chunks, or the relevant information is spread across many documents in a way that needs synthesis, the model can confidently answer from the wrong context. Sometimes it also gets conflicting signals, where what's in its weights disagrees with what's in the prompt, and it's not always predictable which one wins.

So my mental model is: use context and tools for knowledge that changes often or needs to be cited, and update the model when you need a durable change in behavior or capability. In practice, the strongest systems combine both. You fine-tune the model to be good at using tools and reading retrieved documents, and then you let the retrieval layer handle the facts.

r001.rationale: The response discusses retrieval quality and context limits, but does not identify users’ need to know which information to supply as a limitation.

r002.rationale: It mentions retrieval errors, synthesis across documents, and conflicts between retrieved context and model weights, but does not state that retrieved facts can miss how they interact with the model’s other knowledge.

r003.rationale: It says retrieval is flexible and that “you don’t have to retrain anything,” communicating that using tools and context can reduce the need to update the model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's useful to separate two things here. One is factual knowledge, and the other is skills or capabilities. For factual knowledge, context and tools work really well. If I want the model to know about something that happened yesterday, or a paper that came out last week, I can just put that into the context or have the model retrieve it. That's basically what RAG and tool use give you, and I think for most practical applications this is the right approach. It's cheaper, it's more controllable, and you can actually audit where the information came from.

But there are a few places where it starts to break down. The first one is just capacity. Even with these very long context windows we have now, there's a difference between the model having something in its context and the model actually using it well. There's a lot of work showing that retrieval quality degrades as you stuff more into the window, the model gets distracted by irrelevant chunks, and so on. So it's not really a free lunch. You pay for it in inference cost and often in accuracy.

The second limit, and I think this is the more fundamental one, is that context gives you facts but it doesn't really give you skills. If a new programming language or a new library comes out, I can paste the documentation into the context and the model will do okay. But it won't be as fluent as a model that was actually trained on thousands of examples of that code. The same thing with reasoning patterns. You can't really teach a model how to do a new kind of problem by just describing it in the prompt. You can nudge it, but the deep competence comes from training, from the weights.

And then there's a third thing, which is more subtle. The model's priors are frozen. So if the world changes in a way that contradicts what the model learned during pretraining, you get this tension where the context says one thing and the weights say another. In my experience the model doesn't always resolve that in favor of the context. It sometimes falls back on what it believes. So for things that are stable and factual, retrieval is great. For things that require the model to actually behave differently, or to internalize a new domain, I think you still need to update the model, whether that's through continued pretraining or fine-tuning.

So my rough rule of thumb is: if it's information, put it in context. If it's a capability, train for it. And in practice most systems end up needing both.

r001.rationale: The response discusses context capacity and retrieval quality, but does not identify users’ need to know which information to supply as a limitation.

r002.rationale: It says context can conflict with the model’s frozen priors and that the model may fall back on what it already believes instead of following the supplied information.

r003.rationale: It recommends context and retrieval for factual information while reserving model updates for capabilities, communicating that tools can reduce the need for updates.

astra-6.text:
I think context and tools are very useful when the limitation is access to information. If you want the model to answer questions about a document, or you need information that changes frequently, it makes sense to retrieve that information rather than continually update the model weights.

But providing information doesn’t necessarily give the model the ability to use it correctly. You can put everything it needs into the context, and it might still struggle to connect the pieces or solve the problem. Tool use has a similar limitation: the model has to know when to call a tool, what to ask for, and how to interpret the result.

So I would distinguish between missing knowledge and missing capability. There’s overlap, of course, but if the model consistently fails at a task even when you provide the relevant information, adding more context may not help. That’s where training or fine-tuning becomes interesting.

And there’s also an efficiency question. If you’re supplying the same instructions and examples on every request, you might be able to teach that behavior through fine-tuning. I see these approaches as complementary: use context and tools for information that needs to be available at inference time, and update the model when you need to improve how it uses that information.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes missing knowledge from missing capability, but does not clearly identify users’ need to determine what information to supply as a limitation.

r002.rationale: It says the model may struggle to connect supplied information and that tool use requires interpreting results, communicating that retrieved facts may not be integrated effectively.

r003.rationale: It says retrieval can provide changing information instead of continually updating model weights, and presents context and tools as complementary to model updates.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by keeping the model informed. If you want it to have access to the latest information, then context and tools are very useful. You don’t necessarily want to update the model’s weights every time a fact changes. You can retrieve that information and give it to the model when it’s needed.

But having information in the context doesn’t necessarily mean the model can use it reliably. It still has to find the relevant pieces, connect them, and reason about them. And with tools, it needs to know when to call a tool, what to ask for, and how to interpret the result. So you’re still limited by the underlying capabilities of the model.

That’s where I see a role for updating the model. If the issue is missing information, retrieval might solve it. If the issue is that the model consistently struggles with a particular task or behavior, putting more information into the prompt may not be enough. These approaches are complementary, and the interesting question is which part of the problem you’re actually trying to solve.

r001.rationale: The response says the model must find relevant pieces, but does not identify users’ need to know which information to supply as a limitation.

r002.rationale: It says the model must connect relevant information and reason about it, communicating that retrieved facts may need to be related to other knowledge.

r003.rationale: It says weights need not be updated every time a fact changes because new information can be retrieved and supplied when needed.
